title: DISPLACEMENT OF STs IN TIGER RESERVE AREAS
body_text:
The Union Minister of State for Tribal Affairs Shri. Durgadas Uikey informed today in Lok Sabha that the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) is mandated to inquire into complaints regarding the deprivation of rights and safeguards of the Scheduled Tribes which include issues related to alienation, development, atrocities, forest right claims, etc. including displacement of Scheduled Tribes from Tiger Reserve areas on a case-to-case basis and makes appropriate recommendations to the concerned authorities, wherever warranted.
A few representations regarding voluntary village relocation from Tiger Reserves have been forwarded to the NTCA by the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST). It has been clarified that the process of relocation of villages from Core/Critical Tiger Habitats is voluntary as per the provisions of Section 38 V (5) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 2006, and Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006. The National Tiger Conservation Authority (Normative Standards for Tourism activities and Project Tiger) Guidelines, 2012, issued under section 38 O (1) (c) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, are also available in the public domain which clearly outline the principle of voluntary relocation which has been reiterated to all State Governments in different forms, from time to time.
The implementation of village relocation is undertaken by the respective State Governments and Union Territory Administrations in accordance with the prescribed guidelines, and District Level Committees are constituted by the concerned States and Union Territories to facilitate effective implementation. The Guidelines issued by this authority provide for a rehabilitation package for voluntary village relocation, including settlement of rights, agricultural land and house construction etc. The framework also provides for provision of basic amenities and convergence with other Government schemes to ensure that relocated families are able to access welfare and development benefits. The financial assistance for voluntary relocation has been enhanced from ₹10 lakh to ₹15 lakh per family in 2021. Insofar as the Ministry of Tribal Affairs is concerned, the State Governments and UT Administrations have been exhorted to ensure that no rightful beneficiary is deprived of their forest rights, including compliance with Section 4(5) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006, which stipulates that the claimants cannot be evicted or removed from forest land under their occupation till the recognition and verification procedure is complete.
The National Tiger Conservation Authority has reiterated to all Tiger Range States that village rehabilitation shall be completely voluntary and that informed consent of the Gram Sabha and the concerned people shall be obtained before undertaking rehabilitation. The States have been advised to undertake voluntary village relocation in accordance with the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and the guidelines issued by this authority. The National Tiger Conservation Authority (Normative Standards for Tourism activities and Project Tiger) Guidelines, 2012, issued under section 38 O (1) (c) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, are also available in the public domain which clearly outline the principle of voluntary relocation which has been reiterated to all State Governments in different forms, from time to time. Consultations with the Gram Sabha are conducted by the respective State Governments which carry out thorough due diligence which incorporate prior informed consent and voluntariness as enshrined in the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Scheduled Tribes and Other Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006.
In order to ensure transparency of process, the said guidelines recommend that the relocation process could be monitored and implemented by the two committees namely, State Level Monitoring Committee & District Level Implementing Committee which consists of representatives from tribal welfare department too. Accordingly, an institutional mechanism for monitoring voluntary village relocation is already provided under the existing framework, and the concerned State Governments undertake relocation in accordance with the prescribed statutory provisions and guidelines. It is to be informed that there are no reports of involuntary or coerced relocation reported to this authority by the State-level Monitoring Committees and District-level Implementing Committees, which are mandated to oversee the process.
RN/

enrichment.summary: In a Lok Sabha reply, MoS for Tribal Affairs Durgadas Uikey stated that relocation of villages from Core/Critical Tiger Habitats is voluntary under Section 38V(5) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act and Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006. He noted NCST forwards complaints on ST displacement to NTCA, financial assistance for voluntary relocation was raised from ₹10 lakh to ₹15 lakh per family in 2021, and no cases of coerced relocation have been reported by State/District level monitoring committees.
enrichment.context: Tiger reserves in India are managed under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 through the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), which designates Core/Critical Tiger Habitats where human settlements can be relocated only voluntarily to reduce human-wildlife conflict and support conservation. This process intersects with the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, which recognizes the rights of Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers over forest land, and mandates that no eviction can occur until rights recognition is complete (Section 4(5)). This creates a tension often debated in policy circles: conservation-driven relocation versus tribal rights protection, with civil society groups periodically alleging that 'voluntary' relocations are sometimes coerced due to power imbalances, poor compensation, or lack of genuine Gram Sabha consultation. The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST), a constitutional body under Article 338A, plays a watchdog role by inquiring into complaints of rights deprivation, including forced displacement, and recommending remedial action, though it lacks direct enforcement power over conservation authorities like NTCA. The institutional architecture described—State Level Monitoring Committees and District Level Implementing Committees—was strengthened after criticism of tiger reserve relocations, aiming to ensure informed consent and proper rehabilitation packages. The 2021 enhancement of the relocation package from ₹10 lakh to ₹15 lakh per family reflects government efforts to make voluntary relocation more attractive and adequately compensatory, though debates persist about whether financial packages alone address loss of traditional livelihoods, cultural ties to forest land, and social capital.
syllabus_topics: GS Paper 2 - Government Policies and Interventions

prelims_questions.question: Voluntary relocation of villages from Core/Critical Tiger Habitats is governed by which of the following provisions?
options: Section 38V(5) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006
Article 244 of the Constitution and the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996
Section 3 of the Environment Protection Act, 1986
prelims_questions.explanation: The release explicitly cites Section 38V(5) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 as the legal basis for voluntary village relocation from tiger reserves.

prelims_questions.question: As per the Forest Rights Act, 2006, under which section can claimants NOT be evicted from forest land until the rights recognition and verification process is complete?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that Section 4(5) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 stipulates that claimants cannot be evicted or removed from forest land under their occupation till the recognition and verification procedure is complete.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the tension between wildlife conservation objectives and the rights of Scheduled Tribes and forest dwellers in the context of village relocation from tiger reserves in India. Suggest measures to reconcile these competing imperatives.

Examine the institutional mechanisms established under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 to ensure that relocation of tribal communities from Critical Tiger Habitats remains genuinely voluntary. How effective have these mechanisms been?

related_articles.title: Status of forest rights claims
related_articles.relationship: Both releases concern implementation of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 for tribal communities in forest areas; the new release cites Section 4(2) of the FRA as a legal basis for voluntary relocation from tiger reserves, directly tying into the FRA claims status reported in this past release.
